post.title: lockshell: The Cloud LLM Never Needed Your API Key
post.description: How I built lockshell, a local Rust secret broker: cloud LLMs write command templates, the broker resolves keys and executes, values never leave the machine.
post.excerpt: When you tell an AI agent to deploy something, you have probably handed it an API key. lockshell splits the job: the cloud LLM writes a command template with named placeholders, and a local Rust broker resolves the secrets, executes, and redacts the output. The values never leave your machine.
post.content:
Every time I tell a coding agent "deploy this", "run this migration", or "list my issues", I have almost certainly handed it an API key. Pasted into chat, exported into env, captured in a debug log, or held server-side by a tool layer I do not control. Chat transcripts live on the LLM provider's servers. Argv is visible to any process that runs `ps`. Shell history persists on disk.

Here is the premise behind lockshell: the cloud LLM never needed the value in the first place. It only needed to express intent. So the LLM writes a command *template* with named placeholders, and a local broker does the part that requires the secret.

lockshell is that broker: a single Rust binary (v0.1.4, about 1,770 lines across 18 source files, plus a 186-line installer) that resolves placeholders from a local vault, executes the command, and redacts the output before the LLM reads it. Secret values never leave the machine: not into chat context, not onto argv, not into shell history, not into any tracked file.

## The core idea: templates, not values

Instead of this, where the key becomes part of a transcript on someone else's server:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: lin_api_ACTUAL_SECRET" https://api.linear.app/graphql
```

The LLM writes this:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: {{LINEAR_API_KEY}}" https://api.linear.app/graphql
```

The LLM knows the *name* of the secret. The broker knows the value. Three explicit trust boundaries fall out of this, and they are written down in docs/THREAT_MODEL.md: the cloud LLM sees only templates in and redacted output out, the broker exchanges only vault-id and field-name requests with the local vault, and the tool subprocess receives secrets only via env.

## Install

One line on macOS. It detects your CPU arch, pulls the matching binary from GitHub Releases, verifies the SHA-256 checksum, installs to ~/.local/bin, and does not touch your shell rc files.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aryateja2106/lockshell/main/install.sh | bash
```

Or build from source with Rust 1.74+:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/aryateja2106/lockshell && cd lockshell && cargo install --path .
```

## Setup: vault first, then the registry

lockshell does not store secrets itself. v0.1 delegates that to agent-password, an encrypted SQLite vault with the vault key in the macOS login keychain and its own session and approval flow. Add a secret via stdin so the value never hits argv or shell history:

```bash
printf '%s' 'lin_api_...' | agent-password login add linear-api --username arya --url https://linear.app --password-stdin --tag agent
```

Then map a placeholder name to that vault entry:

```bash
lockshell register LINEAR_API_KEY linear-api password
```

That mapping lands in a plain TSV file at ~/.config/lockshell/registry.tsv. Names and vault pointers only, never values. A `lockshell setup` wizard handles first-time configuration. When something is misconfigured, the doctor prints the exact fix commands:

```bash
lockshell doctor --fix
```

## Running a command

```bash
lockshell run --reason "list my issues" -- \
  'curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: {{LINEAR_API_KEY}}" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    --data "{\"query\":\"{ viewer { id name email } }\"}" \
    https://api.linear.app/graphql'
```

docs/PROVIDERS.md has ready-made recipes for Linear, Vercel, Supabase, GitHub, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, and Cloudflare.

### How it works

1.  **Extract**: a regex pulls every {{PLACEHOLDER}} out of the template.
2.  **Audit first**: an entry with the template, the reason, and the secret names (never values) is appended to the audit log before anything runs.
3.  **Resolve**: each placeholder is looked up in the TSV registry, and the broker asks the agent-password vault for the value. Its session, request, approve flow means the broker only reads secrets I have approved for the session.
4.  **Substitute safely**: each {{NAME}} is rewritten to "$NAME", deliberately double-quoted. More on that below.
5.  **Execute**: the command runs as a `/bin/bash -c` subprocess with resolved values passed via `Command::env`. Secrets never appear on argv and are never string-interpolated into the command text. In-process copies are wrapped in `zeroize::Zeroizing`.
6.  **Redact**: stdout and stderr pass through a regex redaction layer for known token formats: Linear, OpenAI, Anthropic, GitHub, Slack, Google, JWTs, AWS access keys. Matches become [REDACTED] before the LLM reads anything. Patterns are user-extensible via ~/.config/lockshell/redactors.txt.
7.  **Exit honestly**: lockshell exits with the child's exit code.

## The audit that found a bug in the security tool

Step 4 says "deliberately double-quoted". That phrasing earned its place. An external code review flagged the original unquoted `$NAME` substitution as a critical shell-injection finding: a secret value containing whitespace or shell metacharacters could break out of its argument boundary. The fix, and the full 11-finding scorecard (1 critical, 1 high, 4 medium, 5 low) with per-finding resolutions, are committed in docs/SECURITY_AUDIT.md.

One more twist: the reviewer was an LLM (gemini-2.5-flash), not a human firm. An AI-safety tool, audited by an AI, publishing the AI's findings. That transparency is worth more than pretending the bug never existed.

## Design decisions I care about

**The two-key nuclear switch.** Disabling redaction requires both the `--no-redact` flag and `LOCKSHELL_ALLOW_NO_REDACT=1` in the environment. The code comment explains why: an agent that mistakenly defaults the flag would otherwise be one config bug away from leaking values.

**Everything on disk is greppable.** Registry, audit log, redactor patterns: all plain TSV, forced to 0700 dirs and 0600 files, re-asserted on every write. Nine direct dependencies. Radical smallness is a trust feature; you can read the whole codebase in an afternoon.

**The audit log never blocks execution.** Auditing is best-effort, not a security gate, because sandboxed agents often cannot write to ~/.config. The broker warns and continues rather than failing closed on logging.

```bash
lockshell audit -n 20
```

**Multi-account is a naming convention, not a feature.** SUPABASE_TOKEN_CLOUDAGI vs SUPABASE_TOKEN_ARYATEJA. No global current-project state, no implicit defaults. The agent picks the account by which placeholder it writes.

```bash
lockshell list --grep supabase
```

**Agents are first-class users.** The repo ships skills/lockshell/SKILL.md, documentation written for AI agents: exit-code semantics (0 proceed, 1 blocker with printed fix commands, 2 non-blocking sandbox issue) and guidance on when the agent must stop and ask the human, such as starting a vault session from inside a sandbox.

**Distrust your own dependency.** Even stderr from the agent-password binary passes through the redactor, in case the vault ever leaks a value into an error string.

A local HTML dashboard shows the registry, recent audit entries, and session state. No daemon, no server:

```bash
lockshell dashboard
```

## Honest limitations

This is a v0.1.x alpha, and the repo's own threat model is blunt about the gaps. I will repeat them here:

- macOS only, with a hard dependency on the external agent-password binary.
- The biometric gate is best-effort today. Upstream agent-password installed via unsigned cargo build silently degrades the Touch ID ACL to plain login-keychain access. A signed native-Keychain backend is planned for v0.3 and does not exist yet.
- No defense against full local compromise. Any process running as your UID can query the vault directly. lockshell keeps secrets out of conversations, not away from an attacker already on your machine.
- Redaction is regex over known token formats. It cannot stop a cloud LLM from exfiltrating sensitive content that a tool legitimately returns.
- The audit log is plain, unsigned TSV. It is not tamper-evident.
- Zeroization is partial: `Command::env` clones secret bytes the code cannot zero, and a source comment admits it.
- There is no automated test suite yet, even though CONTRIBUTING.md tells contributors to run cargo test. That is embarrassing, and it is on the list.
- The installer skips checksum verification with only a warning if it cannot fetch SHA256SUMS.
- The only security review so far was an LLM, not a human firm. A paid third-party review is scheduled before v1.0.
- Zero GitHub stars as of today. There is no adoption story here, only a design story.

Also worth repeating from the threat model: it lists *you* as an adversary. "You typing the secret value into chat anyway. Habits beat tooling." And bad token scope beats any broker: a read-only token is safer than a perfectly brokered full-access one.

## What's next

The public roadmap runs in five phases: single binary (shipped), daemon plus MCP server, signed native Keychain backend, menu bar app, Linux port. None of the later phases exist yet, and the roadmap's own note is "honest timeboxes; multiply by 2 when in doubt".

If you run coding agents against real accounts, try it, grep the TSV files, read the audit doc, and tell me where it breaks. [The code is on GitHub](https://github.com/aryateja2106/lockshell), Apache-2.0.

I built lockshell around one observation: the cloud LLM never needed the value, only the intent.

1. Templates beat trust. The LLM writes {{LINEAR_API_KEY}}, a local Rust broker resolves it from an encrypted vault and executes. Values never enter the conversation.

2. Dangerous flags should need two keys. Disabling output redaction requires a flag AND an env var, so one agent config bug cannot leak values.
